title: Expand local AI reach with Windows ML | OD851

segments.text: ANDREW LEADER: Welcome,
Windows developers and AI experts.
I wanted to start today's session with a survey,
but since I can't see you raise your hands,
click the like button if you've ever opened a cloud invoice
and felt your stomach drop.
You might have experienced this
when adding cloud-backed AI models to your app.
Your users end up loving the feature and use it constantly,
which is awesome, but then you get the bill for all
that cloud resource usage.
What if we could change that story?
What if we could run the same model locally using the hardware
the user already has and still build the same amazing features
that users love without the bill at the end of the day?
Using AI locally means that instead of a bill,
you get better privacy, lower latency, offline support,
and finally those cost savings we mentioned.
Many top ISVs are already using local AI on Windows to delight
and empower their users.
Today, we're going to show you how you can run your own custom
or open-source AI models locally on Windows using Windows ML.
I'm Andrew Leader, a Product Manager on the Windows ML team.
MAHA BAYANA: And I'm Maha Bayana,
and I'm a Software Engineer on the Windows ML team.
ANDREW LEADER: So Maha,
what models can you use with Windows ML?
MAHA BAYANA: So Windows ML works with ONNX models,
meaning you can choose from over 40,000 ONNX models
from Hugging Face, or you could choose
from 229,000 PyTorch models and use the WinML CLI or PyTorch
to convert them to ONNX.
You can also train your own models
to achieve exactly what you need and convert it to ONNX format.
So once you have an ONNX model, you can run it on Windows ML,
but if you want to run it on the best possible across GPU
and NPU, you can even optimize your model for each IHV.
So you can use the WinML CLI to optimize your models,
and then the WinML allows your app to accelerate your models
against a wide variety of Windows hardware
without shipping specific SDKs or each hardware variant.
ANDREW LEADER: That sounds really great.
Some of my users are still on Windows 10, though.
Can I still use Windows ML?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah, of course.
So Windows ML is built for varying needs
on Windows developers supporting operating systems back
to Windows 10.
ANDREW LEADER: That's excellent.
A few of our apps are written in C, though.
Can I use Windows ML with C?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah, of course.
You can use Windows ML directly with C apps.
You can even use Python with Windows ML,
or you can use C Sharp and C++, too.
ANDREW LEADER: That's perfect.
I've got a number of old apps
that I could really use local AI, but the way I package
and deploy them is a little bit outdated.
Can I still use Windows ML regardless
of how I deploy my app?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah, of course.
So Windows ML supports both unpackaged and packaged apps,
and also supports self-contained
and framework-dependent deployment techniques.
So you can truly build your app however you want while
leveraging Windows ML.
ANDREW LEADER: That's amazing.
I'm sold. All right, let's build something.
So in today's session, Maha is going
to be building a customer support sentiment analysis
dashboard that takes our incoming customer support
messages and uses a sentiment analysis model
to classify each message's sentiment into positive,
neutral, and negative buckets
so that we can see the overall trends of our customer feedback
and notice when a negative event is occurring
and react to it quickly.
By the end of this session, you'll learn how
to use Windows ML to convert and optimize a model
from HuggingFace to run on NPU, GPU, and CPU Windows PCs,
and then use that model in a website running inside Edge
or Chrome, and then finally use that same model
in a native Windows app for even better Windows integration.
All right, let's get started.
Maha, can you show us how to use the Windows ML CLI to convert
and optimize a model to run on Windows?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah.
So for those of you who aren't familiar with Windows ML CLI,
it's a new command line tool with a variety
of model conversion and optimization tasks.
So this CLI supports a number of commands.
So let's get over here and let's start
by running our WinML Hub command.
Now, this command helps to see a bunch of models it supports,
and let's go ahead and run this, and it's going
to take a second over there.
All right.
So it looks like there's a sentiment analysis model
over here and that we could use for our tasks.
So let's go ahead and export
that into our project using this export command over here.
So let's go ahead and have that export command, and we're going
to run that, and that's going to take a second.
ANDREW LEADER: Awesome.
And while that's exporting,
can you tell me how you know what all those models are for?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah.
So all of these models are from Hugging Face,
like the one right here,
like the sentiment Twitter analysis model
that we are using.
So you can find the models on there, read their descriptions,
or you could even ask Copilot about them.
ANDREW LEADER: Oh, that's great.
Yeah, I think I can make sense of that.
And this ONNX model, will it work on all Windows PCs?
MAHA BAYANA: Correct.
So this model will work on CPU devices to reach
across all Windows PCs, but can also be accelerated using
like NPUs and GPUs and so on.
ANDREW LEADER: Awesome.
So now that we have an ONNX model,
can we use this in our web app?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah.
So let's open up our web app over here so we can look
at some of the code here.
So this is our customer support dashboard, and the goal
of this app, as you said earlier,
is to classify these incoming customer support comments
and reviews into three different categories, positive,
negative, and neutral.
ANDREW LEADER: Got it.
And which web libraries will be using in this app?
MAHA BAYANA: Okay.
So we're going to be using ONNX Runtime Web,
which essentially lets us use ONNX models and works
with WebNN behind the scenes to run the sentiment model
that we exported earlier using that WinML CLI.
So let's go ahead and see how we can get access
to the ONNX Runtime Web.
So we've already run NPM install ONNX Runtime Web
in this particular project, and then we're going to go up here
to this code at the very top, and we're going
to use this one line over here, which is import ORT
from ONNX Runtime Web.
And this is still an experimental feature,
thus you see that /experimental as a part of it.
So for WebNN, I also enable some developer preview flags
to enable WebNN, since right now it's currently
in developer preview mode.
So we can go ahead to the browser over here,
and as you can see in these flags,
we have these particular WebNN API flags and WebNN flags set
over here in order to use WebNN.
ANDREW LEADER: That's awesome.
Now that we have our prerequisites,
how do we use our model in our web app?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah.
So let's look at some code here again.
Yeah. So first we fetch our model
in this section of the code.
So as you can see over here,
we're basically using the model base path, and we're getting
that model that we initially exported using WinML CLI.
ANDREW LEADER: So that downloads the model
onto the user's device, but then after that it runs locally?
MAHA BAYANA: Correct.
So other than the CDN cost of the initial model download
to the user's device, which we can cache for future reloads,
everything else runs 100% locally on the user's device.
ANDREW LEADER: That's awesome.
I love the sound of that.
So how do we load the model?
MAHA BAYANA: All right.
So to load the model, we need to create an inference session,
and in order to create an inference session,
we're going to start by creating context.
So first, we're going to look at the API over here,
where we're going to basically use the create context API
in order to tell the device what kind of hardware we want to use.
So in this case, we're going to use the CPU.
So we're going to set our device type to CPU.
For step number two, we're going to go ahead
and create our inference session.
Now, in order to create our inference session,
we're going to use this API right over here,
which is ORT.Inference Session.Create.
Now, once we have that API in place,
we want to give it a couple of metrics to specify what kind
of hardware and what kind of EPs we want to use.
So we're going to go ahead and set our EPs to be WebNN,
our context, which we set in the earlier step,
and then we're also going to set those model ONNX data
that we got from our WinML CLI from earlier.
ANDREW LEADER: Excellent.
Is there anything else we need to do before we run this?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah.
And for the rest of the code, essentially,
we're just validating input, tokenizing
and tensorizing the input, and then basically just running it
in the session that we created.
It also runs Softmax on the logits after inference,
and that's essentially just to map these probabilities
into their own sentiment categories.
ANDREW LEADER: Got it.
Sounds great.
Can we run the app and see it work?
MAHA BAYANA: Sure.
Let's do that.
So let's go ahead and run our app.
So we're going to simply do
that by typing the command pythonserver.py.
And once we do that, we can go ahead
and open our local host web app over here.
And, yeah, as you can see, it's going to take a couple
of seconds to load that model and get that EP set up.
But once that happens, we can see the model up in a lot.
As you can see that we have all of these messages
on the right side of the screen,
and these are basically incoming messages
that are being classified into positive, negative, and neutral.
And then to the left of the screen,
you can see that we have a little sentiment analysis chart.
And this is essentially taking each one of those sentiments,
converting them to a chart, so you can kind of see
that sentiment over time.
ANDREW LEADER: That's really excellent.
And so, this is all running on the CPU, though, right?
MAHA BAYANA: Correct.
So how about we make this a little bit faster?
ANDREW LEADER: Yeah, that'd be great.
I heard about these devices that have NPUs.
Can we leverage the newest NPUs with WebNN?
MAHA BAYANA: Of course.
So let's go ahead back a couple of steps.
And remember how we set that create context part?
So we're going to go over there, and we're going
to change our required device type from CPU to NPU.
So once we do that, we're going to go ahead and save the file.
And then we're going to go to our browser and reload our site.
So again, that's going to take a couple of seconds
to load our model and our EP, but we should see it
in just about a moment.
ANDREW LEADER: Wow.
That was a really simple change,
and it's running so much faster now.
This is really awesome.
MAHA BAYANA: Right?
It's so much faster.
As you can clearly see,
it's classifying those incoming messages much faster
into their sentiment categories.
And we also have this chart that's updating
in real time much faster than what it was doing with the NPU.
ANDREW LEADER: Yeah, and the rest
of the device stays responsive
since it's all processing on the NPU.
This is really perfect, but it gives me an idea.
What if we could have a floating overlay
so that this chart is always visible on the top right
of the user's screen, and then our support manager can keep an
eye on things while working on other tasks?
Could we do that?
MAHA BAYANA: Yes, that sounds awesome.
So let's go ahead and use our native WinUI 3 app.
So let's convert this web app into a native WinUI 3 app
in order to get that floating overlay.
ANDREW LEADER: Yeah, and we can use the same ONNX model
with that Windows app?
MAHA BAYANA: Correct.
So you can use the same ONNX model
that we downloaded using the WinML CLI,
pretty much just export it the same way we did before.
All right, so in this WinUI 3 native project,
I've installed the WinApp SDK ML and WinApp SDK runtime packages,
which adds WinML and ONNX runtime to our app.
So as you can see in the packages part of this file,
you can clearly see that we have these packages installed
over here.
ANDREW LEADER: Yeah, and that runtime package,
that adds the Windows App SDK framework-dependent version,
so our app can be smaller and not carry as many binaries?
MAHA BAYANA: Correct.
It saves about 40 MB of binaries
that we'd otherwise have to carry in our app.
ANDREW LEADER: Nice.
Okay, so once we have those installed, what's next?
MAHA BAYANA: So next we have our app install
and register the WinML execution providers.
ANDREW LEADER: Okay, I've heard about execution providers.
I think those are SDKs built by the hardware vendors like AMD,
Intel, NVIDIA, and Qualcomm, and they allow us
to accelerate our models on their NPUs,
GPUs, and CPUs, right?
MAHA BAYANA: Correct.
So WinML allows us
to dynamically acquire these providers,
meaning that our app doesn't need to carry 80 MB
of providers, further reducing our app size
and simplifying our distribution.
ANDREW LEADER: Awesome.
MAHA BAYANA: So we can use a few steps
in our code to acquire these EPs.
So let's go ahead and scroll down to this part over here.
So first, we're going to create our ORT environment using this
particular line over here,
which essentially just creates an ORT environment instance.
So once we've done that, for step number two,
we're going to have to discover the compatible EPs
with our execution-provided catalog.
So we're going to jump down to this particular method
over here, and you can see that we're going
to be using the Find All Providers API in the list
to essentially list all of the execution providers
that are available to us.
Now, for today's session, we're going to be using the QNN EP.
So we're going to see through all
of these execution provider lists that we have in a for loop
and look for our specific EP, which is a QNN one.
So once we have our QNN EP, for step number three,
we're going to go ahead and call EnsureReadyAsync API
on our particular EP.
Now, this is essentially going to help make that EP ready.
And once that EP is ready, we're going to go to step number four,
which is essentially registering that EP to our environment.
So we're going to go ahead and use this API down here,
which is TryRegister in order to register our EP to ONNX Runtime.
ANDREW LEADER: Got it.
And so, if the EPs aren't on the device,
those actually get pulled down through Windows Update.
Is that correct?
MAHA BAYANA: Correct.
ANDREW LEADER: All right.
Now that we have those EPs on the device, how do we inference
against a specific EP?
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah.
So to run a model inference using a specific EP,
we need to use something called as session options.
Now, we can set quite a few metrics in the session options.
So let's go ahead and scroll down to this part,
which essentially sets those metrics.
So over here, we can see that for step number one,
we're kind of using that API called GetEPDevices in order
for it to give us all our EP and device combinations.
So the one that we're going to be using
for today's session is going
to be our QNN EP with the NPU device.
So we're going to see through all of those combinations
over here in order to look for that specific one.
So for step number three, we're going to go ahead
and use our Append Execution Providers API.
And we're essentially going to get that QNN NPU
that we found from earlier.
And we're going to append it to this particular session options.
So we can tell our inference session,
this is what we want you to run on.
And then, we can also set a couple of other options
with our session options.
For example, if I don't want my session to run on the CPU
and I completely want to disable it,
I can use this AddSessionConfigEntry API.
And in this API, as you can see over here,
we're essentially just saying disable the CPU fallback.
And, yeah, you can also use some other APIs
like SetExecutionPolicy or SetEPPolicy.
And that will essentially help you prefer one sort
of hardware over the other.
So in this case, that would be our NPU over the CPU.
ANDREW LEADER: Excellent.
Yeah, that code looks pretty similar to our web code.
It's pretty neat how we can use the ONNX Runtime on both web
and native and share a lot of the code.
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah.
ANDREW LEADER: And so, did you already implement
that pop-out feature we mentioned?
MAHA BAYANA: Yes.
So we can go ahead and click on this button right over here,
which is "Pop-out Overlay".
And you can see that that kind of pops
out a little sentiment chart to the right top of your screen.
Now, the nice thing about this is you can always have it
at the corner of your eye.
So let's say you're talking to Copilot or writing
up some docs, reading your emails.
It's always at the corner of your eye, and you can kind
of keep track of that sentiment over time.
So we can go ahead and click our Word doc over here,
and it's still at the corner of your eye.
ANDREW LEADER: That's perfect.
And it's still running so fast because it's all using the NPU,
and the device still stays performant,
and the CPU isn't getting bogged down.
MAHA BAYANA: Correct.
So we can look at the task manager over here,
and you can clearly see over here that it runs on the NPU.
ANDREW LEADER: That's amazing.
Great work, Maha.
That looks excellent.
MAHA BAYANA: Yeah.
Thank you.
I can't take all the credit for it, though.
Windows ML has definitely made it much,
much easier to use local AI on this device.
ANDREW LEADER: Yeah.
Speaking of what's new with Windows ML in 2026,
we started today with the Windows ML CLI tool,
which is a new tool that helps you convert and optimize models
to run locally on Windows across CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs.
The Windows ML ORT Gen AI library has also received a
number of performance updates,
leading to faster local LLM inferencing on Windows.
And Windows ML itself has been updated to version 2.0,
bringing the ONNX Runtime 1.24, which includes a number
of performance and stability updates,
and some newly updated plugin-based execution providers
that have performance updates and allow you
to use the execution providers
across different runtime versions more easily.
And finally, WebNN is being updated to use Windows ML
when on Windows, as we saw earlier,
leading to faster hardware-accelerated machine
learning model inferencing when on Edge or Chrome browsers.
And if you're looking to try Windows ML for yourself,
you can install the AI Dev Gallery app.
It includes numerous samples
of various AI models running locally via Windows ML,
and it includes code samples,
so you can easily use those models in your own apps.
And finally, I wanted
to highlight some other local AI solutions on Windows.
Windows ML is part of the Microsoft Foundry on Windows,
which provides three main local AI solutions.
If you're not a machine learning expert like Maha,
you should check out the Windows AI APIs in Foundry Local,
both of which provide ready-to-use AI models
that require no machine learning expertise.
These models are pre-optimized and installed system-wide,
allowing you to focus on writing your code rather
than optimizing models.
But if you need something custom that you can't find in AI APIs
or Foundry Local, you can use Windows ML
to run any custom or open-source model.
To learn more about Windows ML, you can visit aka.ms/WindowsML
to see our documentation.
Additionally, we'd love to hear your feedback.
Please email us.
And finally, check out our other sessions at Build 2026,
including Breakout 260, which covers everything
in Microsoft Foundry on Windows.
Thank you all for watching.
We can't wait to see what you build using Windows ML.
MAHA BAYANA: Thank you.
